flawed_step: Step 2: The required greedy-choice assertion—that selecting a maximum-degree vertex preserves the possibility of obtaining a minimum vertex cover—is false.
counterexample: Let V={v,u1,u2,u3,w1,w2,w3} and E={{v,u1},{v,u2},{v,u3},{u1,w1},{u2,w2},{u3,w3}}. Initially deg(v)=3, deg(ui)=2, and deg(wi)=1, so the first greedy choice is legally (indeed uniquely) v. Deleting v and its incident edges leaves the three disjoint edges {ui,wi}. Choose u1,u2,u3 in succession; each is a legal maximum-degree choice because every nonisolated remaining vertex has degree 1. The greedy output is {v,u1,u2,u3}, of size 4. However, {u1,u2,u3} covers every original edge, so a cover of size 3 exists. Moreover, the three pairwise vertex-disjoint edges {v,u1}, {u2,w2}, and {u3,w3} force every vertex cover to contain at least 3 vertices. Thus the minimum cover size is exactly 3, while this legal greedy execution returns 4 vertices.
assessment_summary: The algorithm always produces a vertex cover, but maximum remaining degree is not a safe choice for minimum cardinality. The explicit seven-vertex tree above has a legal greedy execution of size 4 although its minimum vertex-cover size is 3.
